This example uses the **standalone gcorr R package** to estimate heritability
and genetic correlation for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and coronary artery disease
(CAD). It shows three workflows:

- Genome-wide LDSC, GNOVA and SumHer using stored LD scores.
- Chromosome-level analysis using named marker sets.
- Regional HESS/rho-HESS using shared projections from BED genotypes.

The database and EUR reference are reused throughout. Stored LD scores are
sufficient for the first two workflows. HESS processes one region at a time,
so it does not require storing genome-wide LD matrices or eigenvectors.

## Prepare the inputs

Start from the database descriptor and filtered EUR reference used in the
[sparse-LD example](Compute_sparseLD_1000G.html). The reference contains
503 people and uses GRCh37 coordinates. Use compatible gbase and gcorr
installations; these examples use **gcorr R 0.1.5 and native 0.1.4**.
Chromosome sets use compact integer membership throughout fitting. See the
[standalone installation guide](https://psoerensen.github.io/gtools/gsuite/docs/source-package-repository.html).

```{r packages-and-reference}
library(gact)
library(gbase)
library(gcorr)

GAlist <- readRDS("path/to/GAlist_hsa.0.0.1.rds")
Glist <- readRDS("path/to/Glist_1000G_eur_filtered.rds")

# Convert a qgg descriptor using the same genotype files, if needed.
if (!inherits(Glist, "gs_genotypes")) {
  Glist <- gbase::gprep(
    bedfiles=Glist$bedfiles, bimfiles=Glist$bimfiles, famfiles=Glist$famfiles)
}
```

The small helpers below align summary statistics, reference alleles and stored
LD scores, and define the EUR regions. They use `Glist$ldscores` when available,
otherwise the existing scores in the gact database.

```{r workflow-helpers}
work <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "gact-gcorr-example")
dir.create(work, recursive=TRUE, showWarnings=FALSE)
base <- "https://psoerensen.github.io/gact/Document/data/"
files <- c("EUR-fourier-ac125e47.bed", "gcorr_cad_t2d_example.R",
           "gcorr_set_scores.R")
for (name in files) {
  destination <- file.path(work, name)
  if (!file.exists(destination)) {
    download.file(paste0(base, name), destination, mode="wb")
  }
}
source(file.path(work, "gcorr_cad_t2d_example.R"))
source(file.path(work, "gcorr_set_scores.R"))

input <- prepare_gcorr_cad_t2d(
  GAlist, Glist, file.path(work, "EUR-fourier-ac125e47.bed"))

# The remaining analyses use the prepared inputs.
rm(GAlist)
invisible(gc())
```

Here, **GWAS1 is T2D** ([Mahajan et al., 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30297969/))
and **GWAS2 is CAD** ([Nikpay et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26343387/)).
The helper keeps the common GWAS1/GWAS2/GWAS6 marker mask used by the website;
GWAS6 contributes only to marker availability. This leaves **7,221,923 markers**
in **1,702 regions**, with no additional genotype QC filter.

Keep the extracted **`stat$n`**. In this database it is approximately 49,071
for T2D and 40,743 for CAD, using the binary-study information size
`Ncase*Ncontrol/(Ncase+Ncontrol)`. The estimates below use that convention;
they have not been transformed to liability-scale heritability. CAD includes
multiple ancestries, so the EUR reference is an approximation.

## Genome-wide analysis with stored LD scores

LDSC estimates the marginal and cross-trait intercepts. GNOVA uses the fitted
LDSC cross intercept. The SumHer example uses an **illustrative equal-marker
baseline**, with the ordinary scores as its architecture; a different
architecture requires the corresponding tagging scores.

```{r genome-wide-fits}
fit_ldsc <- gcorr_ldsc(
  input$statistics, input$ldscores, input$blocks,
  marker_count=input$reference_marker_count,
  marginal_intercept="free",
  maximum_chi_square=max(
    .001 * max(vapply(input$statistics, function(x) max(x$n), numeric(1))), 80))

fit_gnova <- gcorr_gnova(
  input$statistics, input$blocks, input$ldscores,
  overlap_intercepts=fit_ldsc$matrices$ldsc_intercept)

architecture <- matrix(
  unname(input$ldscores), ncol=1,
  dimnames=list(names(input$ldscores), "baseline"))
fit_sumher <- gcorr_sumher(
  input$statistics, architecture,
  c(baseline=input$reference_marker_count), input$ldscores, input$blocks,
  reference_sample_size=input$Glist$n, inflation="multiplicative")

fit_ldsc$estimates
fit_gnova$estimates
fit_sumher$estimates
```

The observed results are shown as **estimate ± standard error**.

<div class="gcorr-table">

| Method | T2D h² | CAD h² | Genetic correlation |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| LDSC | 0.470 ± 0.025 | 0.311 ± 0.019 | 0.384 ± 0.028 |
| GNOVA | 0.498 ± 0.028 | 0.111 ± 0.019 | 0.604 ± 0.059 |
| SumHer baseline | 0.488 ± 0.029 | 0.362 ± 0.023 | 0.387 ± 0.027 |

</div>

LDSC and this SumHer baseline give very similar genetic correlations and T2D
heritabilities. CAD heritability differs more, particularly for GNOVA, which
uses a unit marginal noise baseline while the other two fits estimate
intercepts or scalings. These are examples conditional on the supplied
statistics, reference and model assumptions.

## Chromosomes as marker sets

Define each chromosome as a named set of marker IDs and fit the sets jointly.
Chromosomes allow us to reuse the ordinary LD scores, assuming negligible LD
between chromosomes. Other annotations with LD across set boundaries require
annotation-specific LD scores.

```{r chromosome-sets}
first <- input$statistics[[1]]
sets <- split(first$rsids, paste0("chr", first$chr))
sets <- sets[paste0("chr", 1:22)]

set_input <- prepare_gcorr_set_scores(
  first$rsids, input$ldscores, sets, marker_counts=lengths(sets))
fit_sets <- gcorr_ldsc_partitioned(
  input$statistics, set_input$annotation_ld_scores, input$ldscores,
  set_input$annotation_sums, input$blocks,
  annotation_overlap=set_input$annotation_overlap,
  reference_sample_size=input$Glist$n,
  reference_marker_count=set_input$reference_marker_count,
  corrected=FALSE, marginal_intercept="free", overlap_intercept=0)

head(fit_sets$estimates)
fit_sets$matrices$category_genetic_covariance
fit_sets$matrices$category_genetic_correlation
```

This example assumes no shared CAD/T2D participants and fixes the cross-trait
intercept to zero. That also excludes a cross-trait confounding intercept,
so its totals can differ from the freely estimated genome-wide fit.

The first five chromosomes and the joint-model total illustrate the output
(estimate ± standard error):

<div class="gcorr-table">

| Set | T2D h² | CAD h² | Genetic correlation |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| chr1 | 0.0325 ± 0.0056 | 0.0287 ± 0.0041 | 0.607 ± 0.087 |
| chr2 | 0.0420 ± 0.0080 | 0.0330 ± 0.0048 | 0.467 ± 0.085 |
| chr3 | 0.0419 ± 0.0063 | 0.0213 ± 0.0050 | 0.651 ± 0.068 |
| chr4 | 0.0264 ± 0.0055 | 0.0133 ± 0.0038 | 0.642 ± 0.159 |
| chr5 | 0.0252 ± 0.0065 | 0.0113 ± 0.0023 | 0.583 ± 0.169 |
| **All 22 chromosomes** | **0.506 ± 0.029** | **0.324 ± 0.021** | **0.568 ± 0.026** |

</div>

Set heritabilities and covariances sum to the joint-model total; correlations
do not. Some chromosome correlations are imprecise, and three raw ratios
exceed one. The plot retains these estimates and their approximate 95% intervals.

![Heritability and genetic correlation across all 22 chromosome sets](data/gcorr-chromosome-set-results.png)

## Regional HESS and rho-HESS

For regional analysis, prepare the projections once for all supplied traits.
gcorr reads each region from the BED reference, shares its decomposition across
traits, and retains compact moments for fitting. Large matrices and
eigenvectors are discarded after each region.

Start with chromosome 22 to check the workflow:

```{r chromosome-pilot}
regions22 <- input$regions[grepl("^chr22_", names(input$regions))]
projection22 <- gcorr_prepare_hess(
  input$statistics, input$Glist, regions=regions22, nthreads=4)

fit22 <- gcorr_fit_hess(
  projection22, c("GWAS1", "GWAS2"),
  shared_sample_size=0, phenotypic_correlation=0)
head(fit22$estimates)
```

The pilot's total describes a chromosome-only model. For genome-wide totals,
prepare all regions together so the joint correction covers the whole genome:

```{r genome-hess}
projection <- gcorr_prepare_hess(
  input$statistics, input$Glist, regions=input$regions, nthreads=4)

fit_hess <- gcorr_fit_hess(
  projection, c("GWAS1", "GWAS2"),
  shared_sample_size=0, phenotypic_correlation=0)
fit_hess$estimates[fit_hess$estimates$component == "total", ]

# Fit a single prepared trait without recomputing LD or eigenvectors.
fit_t2d <- gcorr_fit_hess(projection, "GWAS1")
```

The automatic rank budget selects at most 11 components per region for these
genome-wide inputs. Truncation improves conditioning but discards signal.
Inspect `projection$rank_policy` and `fit_hess$diagnostics$conditioning` when
applying this workflow to other data. To reuse it in a later session, save the
compact object with `saveRDS(projection, "hess-projection.rds")`.

### Interpret the HESS results

At the original Z scale, CAD heritability is close to zero and poorly
determined, giving a genetic-correlation ratio above one. This ratio cannot
be interpreted as a biological correlation.

The CAD paper reports genomic control at cohort and final meta-analysis
levels. We can illustrate sensitivity to its final factor of 1.18 using the
same saved moments:

```{r hess-sensitivity}
fit_sensitivity <- gcorr_fit_hess(
  projection, c("GWAS1", "GWAS2"),
  shared_sample_size=0, phenotypic_correlation=0,
  genomic_control=c(GWAS1=1, GWAS2=1.18),
  genomic_control_provenance=c(
    GWAS1="Unchanged T2D Z scale",
    GWAS2=paste("Sensitivity: final CAD meta-analysis factor 1.18;",
                "earlier cohort corrections have not been reconstructed")))
fit_sensitivity$estimates[
  fit_sensitivity$estimates$component == "total", ]
```

<div class="gcorr-table">

| HESS input scale | T2D h² | CAD h² | Genetic correlation |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Original | 0.274 ± 0.018 | 0.013 ± 0.028 | 1.221 ± 0.333* |
| Partial CAD adjustment | 0.274 ± 0.018 | 0.168 ± 0.024 | 0.371 ± 0.021 |

</div>

\*The out-of-range ratio has only a descriptive jackknife SE.
The partial adjustment is a **sensitivity analysis**, conditional on the stored
release using that final correction. Earlier cohort corrections remain
unresolved. It is not a validated full correction. The current HESS default
uses the original software variance equations for h²/covariance and a regional
jackknife for genome-wide correlation.

## Observed time and memory

These examples were rerun with **gcorr R 0.1.5/native 0.1.4**, R 4.4.1,
Windows 11, an Intel Core i7-1365U and 16 GB RAM. Each step used a separate
R process, with no concurrent builds or analyses. The native OpenMP maximum
was four; HESS decoding and matrix products used four threads. Input loading and output saving
are excluded from the times.

Memory is resident memory for the **entire R process**, sampled every 200 ms.
“Before” is measured after loading the required inputs and garbage collection;
“Peak” is the maximum during that step. Both include marker metadata and
statistics. These workers do not load `GAlist`. The chromosome row includes
matching sets to integer indices and fitting with compact scores.

<div class="gcorr-table">

| Step | Time | Before (GiB) | Peak (GiB) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| LDSC fit | 9.3 s | 1.53 | 3.02 |
| GNOVA fit | 6.4 s | 1.54 | 3.09 |
| SumHer baseline fit | 12.9 s | 1.58 | 3.53 |
| Chromosome sets and fit | 29.9 s | 1.60 | 3.27 |
| HESS preparation | 15 min 21 s | 2.34 | 5.76 |
| HESS pair fit: original scale | 4.0 s | 0.12 | 0.38 |
| HESS pair fit: partial adjustment | 3.4 s | 0.12 | 0.43 |

</div>

HESS prepares the regional projections once. Both pair fits above reuse these
new projections. Resident memory excludes paged allocations; it is a process
measurement, not the size of the numerical solver alone.
